turns.q:
Your response was: "Looked at it. Checkout flow. Nearly missed the submit button. It barely registered visually — took a moment to find the action I needed."

We want to understand what you meant by "nearly missed the submit button", so let's go a bit deeper. Which of these best captures what you were pointing at?

A) The visual hierarchy is inverted, with the secondary "Continue Shopping" button appearing much more prominent than the primary "Place Order" action.
B) The "Place Order" button is visually greyed out or muted compared to the rest of the interface, making it look inactive or disabled.
C) The placement of the "Place Order" button at the very bottom of the page, separated from the payment fields by a large gap, makes it easy to overlook.
D) None of the above — but only if A, B, and C genuinely miss what you meant (you must still name the specific element you were referring to)

Select A, B, C, or D to continue.
What specific visual cues in the "Place Order" button—such as its light grey background or lighter text color—signal to you that it is inactive rather than just a secondary action?
turns.a: Lighter one disappeared into the background. Almost looked inactive.

turns.q: If a user assumed the button was disabled because it blended in, would they likely abandon the checkout or try to find an alternative way to submit their order?
turns.a: 'Place Order.' Faint. Label barely there. Easy to overlook — didn't register where it should.

turns.q: If the label is that faint, what specific visual element or layout cue would a user need to see to confirm that this muted button is actually the primary action they are supposed to take?
turns.a: Same. Eye went elsewhere. Didn't pull.

turns.q: If that button were visually distinct enough to stop your eye, would the concern about it looking inactive disappear, or is there something else in its placement that still feels wrong?
turns.a: More visible. Bigger. Has to stand out — can't be the one you scan past.

turns.q: If the design team could only change one structural thing about that button's visual weight before development, what specific adjustment would make it impossible to scan past?
turns.a: Solid high-contrast fill on 'Place Order' — a real color, not gray. WCAG AA minimum: 4.5:1 contrast ratio for the label text. Label up to at least 14–16px. Gray on gray at 12px reads as disabled — it fails WCAG AA and it fails as a primary CTA. Fix: brand color fill, white label text, readable size. One button. That's it.
